cards.title: Agency exit multiples: what drives valuation
cards.summary: An agency owner breaks down the factors behind exit multiples, from client quality to retention and growth trajectory.
cards.use_when: Evaluating an agency or service business for sale, or planning an exit strategy for a services firm.
steps: Recognize that a small design/build web or app agency might command 3–5x profit, but recurring or retained revenue pushes the multiplier up.
Lock in long-term contracts: predictable revenue 9 months out increases the multiple because buyers can forecast cash flow.
Build a roster of hard-to-get, prestigious clients — the difficulty of replicating those relationships raises enterprise value.
Demonstrate strong retention (e.g., 90% retained revenue) and consistent growth in the years before exit; the source grew the business 2.5x from COVID to 18 months post-COVID and secured 11x profit.
Aim for scale or a strategic acquirer who can open doors to much larger contracts, as happened in the earnout year when individual contracts exceeded the entire previous agency revenue.
Time the market: the source sold in 2021, described as an ideal seller's market, though timing is not fully controllable.
caveats: Multiples are highly situational; 11x is described as absurdly high for an agency and not a target.
Shouldn't think about exit multiples as a beginner — focus on creating cash flow and learning lessons first.

cards.title: Compounding returns of long-term specialization
cards.summary: A strategy for maximizing wealth: do what you're good at for an extremely long period to become world-class, rather than chasing fast money.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate time and energy across ventures, especially when tempted by quick-return opportunities like crypto or speculative investing.
steps: Identify the activity you're already good at and commit to doing it for an 'insane period of time' — the source's agency took 10 years (age 21 to 30) to build.
Expect that the real payoff is not a short spike but a prolonged compound effect; the source warns that private-equity-style fast wealth is a trap that distracts from your core work.
Avoid getting seduced by crypto, meme coins, or investment schemes; the source notes these take your eye off the ball and require different, equally difficult skills.
If you get bored and want fulfillment outside of money, deliberately pivot — but recognize that big money and big fulfillment may pull in different directions.
Focus on continuous learning through direct conversations with people who have walked the path; the source credits talking to experienced people as the most important learning method.
caveats: The 'do it for an insane period' advice is aimed at maximizing money; the source explicitly says if you want fulfillment, do something else.
Survivorship bias is real — for every Doc Martens-style scaled success, there are many bad stories.

cards.title: Build in public: how a speech impediment became a YouTube presence
cards.summary: A creator's method for overcoming public-speaking anxiety by starting on camera, then translating that to live leadership.
cards.use_when: Founders or operators who struggle with public speaking, video content, or addressing teams and need a desensitization approach.
steps: Force exposure to the medium you fear: the source had a speech impediment and made himself get in front of a camera, even getting drunk for his first video.
Use a low-stakes format like YouTube or Zoom to build fluency before attempting live audiences; the source initially addressed his company only via Zoom with the camera off.
Seek out people who uplift you in the specific area you're weak in; the source credits two weeks with an experienced presenter who reframed nerves as unnecessary comparison.
After internalizing the reframe ('I have my own great story'), seize the next natural moment to perform live — the source addressed 40 people the day after a flight, without prior rehearsal.
Notice the environment effect: being around someone who makes you feel capable raises your performance, while critics make you retreat; choose your circle deliberately.
caveats: The source's first video method (drinking to speak) is a personal anecdote, not a recommended tactic for others.
Public-speaking progress was gradual and situational, not a one-off fix.

cards.title: Do what you're good at, not what you're passionate about (early on)
cards.summary: A reframe of the 'follow your passion' advice: build competency and profit first, then pursue passion once financially free.
cards.use_when: Giving or receiving career advice for young people or early-stage founders, especially when choosing between a passion project and a practical income path.
steps: Recognize that billionaires who say 'follow your passion' already have the financial liberty to do so; their advice isn't practical for beginners.
If you follow your passion before achieving success, you'll likely fail and lose the ability to continue that passion — it becomes unsustainable.
Instead, deliberately become passionate about success metrics: the first sale, the first profit, the first cash flow.
Use that momentum to build a stable financial base, after which you can pursue whatever you want because money is no longer the constraint.
Apply the same logic to business choices: prioritize opportunities based on learning speed and cash flow over personal interest when starting out.
caveats: This is presented as advice for making money; if fulfillment is your goal, the source says to do something else.
Not a universal rule — some people may thrive by pursuing passion directly, though the source argues against it for young people.

cards.title: Billionaire habits: the one common denominator
cards.summary: Observing that sustained, long-term ambition to create money is the only consistent trait among billionaires; other factors vary widely.
cards.use_when: Analyzing high-net-worth individuals or deciding whether extreme wealth accumulation is the right goal for you.
steps: Look past product genius, work hours, or biohacking routines — the source found these differ greatly among billionaires.
Identify the common thread: they have all been doing it for a very long time and have never relented in their ambition to create money.
Accept that this single-minded pursuit may be 'boring' and not necessarily appealing if you value other things like family, hobbies, or a relaxed lifestyle.
Recognize that for those with massive wealth, the driver is often ego and curiosity rather than money itself, so more wealth doesn't change behavior.
Use this to self-assess: if you aren't willing to chase money relentlessly for decades, you likely won't become a billionaire — and that may be fine.
caveats: Based on the source's personal observation of billionaires, not a controlled study.
The source acknowledges he could be a billionaire but chooses not to, implying the trait is necessary but not sufficient.

cards.title: Fake it till you make it: situational and growth-oriented
cards.summary: A nuanced take on imposter syndrome and exaggeration: useful when non-malicious and directed toward building real capability.
cards.use_when: When feeling insecure in a new role or venture, or when assessing whether to project confidence you don't yet feel.
steps: Acknowledge that many successful entrepreneurs exhibited some exaggeration when growing up — to win clients, build an audience, or close deals.
Use self-talk or external projection as a temporary state to reduce anxiety and enter a more confident frame, as the source does by reminding himself of past achievements.
Ensure the exaggeration isn't malicious or a zero-sum exploitation of others; it should be about stretching into a future self.
Often you end up growing into the claim or surpassing it, so the gap closes over time.
Shift your focus: consciously care about different things, and the need to fake it diminishes.
caveats: The source draws a line at malicious or exploitative deception.
The source also notes he has moved toward 100% truthfulness and confronting why he cares what others think as a better long-term approach.

cards.title: Two foundations for reduced anxiety: truthfulness and confronting approval-seeking
cards.summary: The source's personal practices for greater peace: living 100% truthfully and examining why you care about others' opinions.
cards.use_when: Founders or high-performers experiencing anxiety, insecurity, or people-pleasing that affects decision-making.
steps: Commit to telling the truth 100% of the time; you may annoy people, but you'll never have to worry about what you said or keep track of lies.
Regularly ask yourself why you care what other people think, and interrogate the answer — you often find the reason is irrelevant or unhelpful.
When anxious, use deliberate self-affirmation ('you've done this, you're great') to shift state, but recognize these are thoughts, not beliefs, if you still feel insecure.
Eliminate 'fake it till you make it' as a default mode as you mature; the source moved from faking to truthfulness as a source of stability.
caveats: These are personal practices from the source's experience, not clinical advice.
Truthfulness may have social costs; the source accepts that trade-off.
